name: Ndun
catalog_citation: Blench, Roger. n.d. [printout 4 Sept 2007]. The Ndun language of Central Nigeria and its affinities. Draft ms circulated for comment, Mallam Dendo, Cambridge (the Internet Archive 2015 capture of rogerblench.info). Companion mss: Blench, The Nyeng language of Central Nige…
catalog_locator: Ndun ms sec. 3.3 Tones, pp. 2-3; Nyeng ms sec. 3.3 Tones, p. 3; Shakara ms sec. 3.3 Tones, p. 3
catalog_quote: [Ndun, 3.3 Tones] Ndun appears to have two tones, high and low in most words. There are also rising and falling tones. However, there are a significant number of words that seem to have a mid-tone on the last syllable, following a high-low sequence. This appears to be conditioned and therefore it is probably not worth setting up a phonemic mid-tone. Nonetheless, for the moment, three tones are marked, pending further elicitation. In this transcription, the mid tone is left unmarked. ... [Nyeng, 3.3 Tones] Nyeng appears to have two tones, high and low. In this transcription, the low tone is left unmarked. There are also rising and falling tones, illustrated by the word ‘thorn’ ... [Shakara, 3.3 Tones] The tone system of Shakara has only two tones and the majority of words appear all low tone. A few possible cases of glide tones occur. Low tone is left unmarked.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: all three deciding passages are verbatim at the cited sections/pages of the held Blench mss, and the absence of any stress/accent sentence is confirmed by a full-text search for stress/accent. The deciding source is a set of draft comparative wordlists with short phonology front matter — thin by genre — but it is first-hand specialist fieldwork and, per Glottolog (0 descriptive refs), the the Internet Archive inventory of Blench's Ndunic folder, Wikipedia's reference list and Blench 2018's bibliography, it is the only description of these lects that exists. Blench 2018 (downloaded, open access) independently restates tonal plural formation in Ndun and says nothing about stress, consistent with the 'tonal, no stress rule stated' coding. sources.quote: No stress/accent statement (a full-text search for stress/accent: zero hits for 'stress'/'accent' in the chapter). On Ndun: 'there are also numerous plurals created by tonal change and by presence and absence of labialisation and palatalisation... The tones are too insecurely marked to be sure that there are no additional contrasts on the V- prefixes.' Cites Rueck et al. (2008) sociolinguistic survey for the Ahwai cover name.
